heading: Extra student neurons reduce getting stuck at poor solutions in shallow ReLU teacher–student networks
definition: in two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems where a perfect solution exists, gradient descent from standard initialization ends in spurious local minima more often as teacher and student grow together, and giving the student one or two more neurons than the teacher sharply reduces or removes this within the tested widths (6 to 20 neurons; Safran & Shamir 2018).
summary: Several independent groups reproduce increasing trapping as equally wide teachers and students grow, and improved training with extra student width under modified procedures. These shallow teacher–student studies do not establish that extra width always eliminates trapping.

suggested_status.by_scale: R2 in shallow teacher-student toy models for increasing equal-width difficulty and the student-width benefit. counts: versions.V2.studies_by_size contains only 'not stated', so parameter-count scale levels cannot be assigned.
suggested_status.reason: The original baseline (arXiv:1712.08968#R1, arXiv:1712.08968#R12) is independently supported under modified recipes: arXiv:2604.09412#R9 and arXiv:2604.09412#R10 reproduce the equal-width trend and extra-neuron benefit; arXiv:2609.09595#R1, arXiv:2609.09595#R2 and arXiv:2609.09595#R3 support increasing matched-width failure; arXiv:1806.01845#R2, arXiv:1806.01845#R10, arXiv:1806.01845#R11 and arXiv:1806.01845#R12 support a fixed-teacher width benefit with incomplete success. At teacher width 20 and student widths 20–22, arXiv:2604.09412#R4 qualitatively supports improved escape with extra width. Persistent trapping is compatible with V2's reduction alternative; unreported convergence frequencies leave the magnitude unresolved rather than establishing a scope limitation. counts: versions.V2.verdicts.supports.studies = 5; versions.V2.verdicts.limits_scope.studies = 2; versions.V2.verdicts.challenges.studies = 0; versions.V2.tested_sharing_an_author_with_an_original = 0. These supplied counts precede the checker's reclassification of R4 from limits_scope to supports and have not been recomputed. R2 applies to these components, without establishing exact-protocol replication or universal elimination of trapping.
suggested_status.open_questions: An independent sweep matching the original GD, Xavier initialization, and endpoint verification would establish exact-protocol reproducibility. Complete two-extra-neuron frequencies and reconciliation of the later study's gradient-flow and GD tables would clarify when trapping is reduced versus empirically absent.

source.title: Spurious Local Minima are Common in Two-Layer ReLU Neural Networks

original_result.setup: Safran and Shamir ran gradient descent on expected squared loss from Xavier initialization, using 1,000 runs per setting and step size 0.1.
original_result.result: With equal teacher and student widths, convergence near suboptimal local minima rose from 0.3% at width 6 to 94% at width 20. For a teacher of width 19, adding one student neuron reduced this frequency from 93.4% to 49.1%.
original_result.interpretation: This is the displayed original-result block, not a guarantee that the original tested every part of this claim.

sources.headline: Wider students reached global optima more often when learning an 11-neuron teacher.
SGD converged to non-global minima with positive loss in equal-width two-layer ReLU networks.
Making the student four times wider reduced high-loss trapping when imitating a shallow ReLU teacher.
Widening equally wide teacher–student networks increased convergence to suboptimal minima; extra student neurons sharply reduced it.
Equally wide ReLU students reached global minima less often as teacher and student widths grew.
Extra student neurons improved optimization, but most runs still failed to reach global optima.
Extra student neurons helped training escape high-loss traps, but trapping persisted at teacher width 20.

wording_issues.issue: Global-optimum hitting frequency and finite-time imitation loss do not establish that unsuccessful runs end at spurious stationary minima. The fixed-teacher SGD study therefore supports a width benefit more directly than it supports this endpoint description.

The strongest independent width-matched evidence uses population gradient-flow/mean-field ODE dynamics. Other supporting endpoints use SGD. These results do not independently reproduce the precise original optimization and initialization recipe.

For an orthonormal teacher of width 17 and student width 19, Table 1 reports 99.63% global convergence over 10^4 initializations under the population gradient-flow/mean-field ODE recipe. Table 2 separately reports 77.50% for GD at the same widths; the discrepancy is unexplained. At teacher width 20 and student widths 20–22, Figure 4 qualitatively shows improved escape and persistent high-loss plateaux, without convergence frequencies. The sharpness of that reduction cannot be determined; persistent trapping is compatible with the claim's reduction alternative. The original's empirical non-observation does not establish universal elimination.

method_sensitivity.what: Joint width growth and widening only the student have different effects. The gradient-flow sweep reports increasing trapping at equal widths and reduced trapping with one extra student neuron. The fixed-teacher SGD sweep improves success with width while retaining substantial failures.

In the ReLU matched-width sweep with Gaussian inputs, D = 2 and M = N in {2, 4, 8, 16}, training combines gradient flow with subsequent second-order optimization. Maximally dissimilar teachers generally have the highest global-minimum success, standard teachers intermediate success, and minimally dissimilar teachers the lowest. Success uses L < 10^-18; unsaved unfinished runs are excluded. This geometry ranking alone does not establish V2's width effect. The separate matched-width trend is decreasing success as width increases; no extra-student-neuron comparison is provided.
